catalog_quote: There are no accentless words in Hamar, and there is only one prominent syllable per word, cued by high pitch, loudness and increased duration. ... Hamar has two co-existing, yet independent systems which can be analysed in terms of stress and tone. ... Stress in nouns is lexical and its position is not predictable. In disyllabic nouns, either the final or the penultimate syllable can be stressed. In disyllabic nouns composed of a heavy syllable, stress is attested in any position: shaa.lá ‘ceiling’ zíi.ga ‘spinal cord’ síl.qa ‘knuckle’ gur.dá ‘village’ Stress in nouns can be lexically distinctive. A few σ́σ vs. σσ́ minimal pairs occurring in the same grammatical domain have been attested: ... átti ʻbirdʼ attí ʻfermented sorghum’ ... Trisyllabic nouns can have a final, penultimate or antepenultimate stressed syllable as displayed in the CV.CV.CV minimal pairs below. ánqasi ‘bee’ anqási …

new_statements.quote: The position of the accent is not sensitive to syllable weight: the heavy syllables CVV and CVC [...] do not always attract accent. [...] Accent in nouns is thus unpredictable and lexically distinctive [...] Different from nouns, accent is not lexical in verbs. Hamar verb roots are accent-less but they always occur with verbal suffixes which bear the culminative accent on the verbal word. This means that the accent is always found on the verbal suffix and never on the verb root. [...] On nouns and verbs accent is culminative and obligatory, showing stress-like properties. Accent is lexically contrastive in any word position in nouns, whereas it is grammatical in verbs.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Hamar (catalog-all-2026-09-12) has an empty rule and there are no existing statements; this paper supplies the rule: lexically contrastive, weight-insensitive accent in nouns, suffix-final grammatical accent in verbs, one prominence per word, system between stress and tone.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Every word has exactly one prominent syllable (accent is obligatory and culminative; accentless words are unattested), realized by higher F0, greater duration and intensity; the syllable is the TBU. In nouns the accent is lexical and unpredictable: it can fall on any syllable (antepenult, penult or final in trisyllables; minimal pairs átti 'bird' / attí 'fermented sorghum') and is not sensitive to syllable weight; plural -na and feminine -no do not move it. In verbs the root is accentless and the accent always sits on the inflectional suffix (citation/imperative form pug-á 'blow!'), i.e. on the rightmost edge of the verb word; some tenses differ only by accent placement within the suffix (qan-átine past neg vs qan-atíne present neg). Petrollino classes the system as 'intermediate' between stress and tone in Hyman's typology (stress-like culminativity/obligatoriness plus a H vs HL pitch contrast on final syllables).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None: 'There is only one prominent syllable per word in Hamar (19a, 19b), and accent-less words are not attested (19c)' (p. 293); no secondary stress is mentioned.
new_statements.exceptions: Masculine gender suffix -â shifts prominence to the final syllable with a falling pitch (CV́.CV > CV.CV̂), but nouns with initial lexical accent may keep it alongside the suffix accent (CV́.CV̂), 'exceptions to culminativity', variation 'highly irregular.. across speakers and within the same speaker's speech' (p. 298); H vs HL opposition on the last syllable of imperative vs negative present (pug-é / pug-ê, p. 297); mid-vowel height is only a partial cue to accent location (p. 290-291).
new_statements.identity_note: Petrollino 2019 describes 'the Hamar variety' of the Hamar-Banna cluster (Hamar, Banna, Bashaɗɗa are mutually intelligible with minor lexical/phonological differences), based on c. 200 words from first-hand data collected in Hamar territories in 2013-2014; the SAL 2024/2025 paper is likewise Hamar (South Omotic, SW Ethiopia). The 2023 chapter is presumably the same variety but was not opened.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: every fragment of the deciding quotation, the domain quote and the exceptions quote is verbatim in the extracted text we hold of Petrollino 2016 at the recorded pages (pp. 40-42, 47, 49-52); locator correct after the stage-C fix. (2) Deciding source: a 2016 fieldwork reference grammar (Leiden PhD = Köppe Cushitic and Omotic Studies 6, confirmed on the Leiden repository record), Glottolog's top and only 'grammar' entry, with an instrumented prosody section; it is the best available description. (3) The one additional dedicated prosody study, Petrollino 2019 (LangSci, open access), was downloaded to and read: it restates that accent is obligatory, culminative, weight-insensitive and 'lexically contrastive in any word position in nouns', grammatical in verbs, with tone-like H/HL contrasts confined to verbal suffixes and masculine-noun
